The visual direction

SlopArena visual identity

SlopArena’s visual identity is an authored collision of scavenged low-poly characters and bold DIY fight graphics. It should look like somebody assembled an underground tournament from cheap assets, questionable ideas, and surprisingly good taste.

The roughness is visible. The decisions underneath it are precise.

1 Overall impression

At first glance, SlopArena should read as a fighting game: strong poses, recognizable weapons, confident typography, decisive shapes.

Then you notice the stupidity—the character premise, an improvised venue, a crude symbol, a dry warning label. That order matters:

“That character looks cool.” → “Wait, what the fuck is that?” → “I want to play them.”

It is neither straight-faced competitive branding nor pure parody. The characters take their fights seriously, even when their existence is ridiculous.

2 Character design

The 3D direction favors:

  • Simplified, visibly low-poly forms.
  • Exaggerated proportions and distinctive silhouettes.
  • Strong costume and body-color groupings.
  • Weapons and props readable from the gameplay camera.
  • Clear poses rather than detail doing all the expressive work.

Every fighter needs a recognizable visual idea. A hairstyle, head shape, stance, enormous weapon, unusual body proportion, or dominant color should identify them before small details become visible.

Different asset sources are acceptable. Different levels of visual importance are not. One character should not look like a hyperreal cinematic hero while another looks like an unfinished background prop.

“Toy-like” means chunky, expressive, and plausibly assembled from unlikely pieces. It does not demand literal toys, plastic shaders, or cute faces.

3 Arenas and world

Arenas should feel like places somebody decided to fight in, not interchangeable fantasy battlegrounds.

Rooftops, industrial junk, strange pools, nighttime urban spaces, or a child’s tabletop can all fit. Each needs one memorable premise or landmark—not a room full of equally loud props.

The visual hierarchy is:

Fighters and attack tells → playable surfaces and edges → the place around the fight.

Character colors can be vivid. Backgrounds can be dirtier, quieter, or more atmospheric. But “grimy” is a supporting quality, not a filter applied to every asset.

Lighting, scale, material response, and composition make the collage coherent. We do not need to rebuild every asset in one bespoke style.

4 Graphic identity

The graphic layer is what turns “a collection of low-poly assets” into SlopArena. It should feel like a fight flyer that became interactive.

Its vocabulary is:

  • Heavy, blocky Archivo Black declarations.
  • Hard rectangular boundaries and flat color fields.
  • Offset-print shadows and thick structural edges.
  • Character cutouts crossing frames.
  • Pasted strips, stamps, crude annotations, and occasional irregular framing.
  • Asymmetrical compositions built on an underlying grid.

Think skate/punk flyers and improvised tournament signage—not polished esports broadcasts.

A panel may look cut out by hand. Its controls still align. A sticker may sit crooked. A settings label does not.

5 Color and typography

The shared graphic palette has distinct jobs:

ColorRole
Dark inkStructure, framing, and calm backgrounds
Warm paperLight fields, labels, and readable contrast
Action Yellow #FFCC22Primary actions and current selection
OrangeImpact, interruption, and combat energy

This is not the complete world palette. Fighters retain signature colors; gameplay retains functional distinctions.

Typography follows the same hierarchy:

TypefaceRole
Archivo BlackName mark, menu declarations, fighter names, major outcomes
Space MonoCompact marketing instructions, metadata, dry annotations
Readable sansDense settings and HUD information

The identity comes from contrast between declaration and instruction, not twenty expressive fonts competing for attention.

6 Imagery and motion

Character artwork can be illustrated or rendered, but it must depict the same fighter as the model: same proportions, costume, weapon, colors, and chunky construction.

Splash art should make the actual character more compelling—not promise a glossy, hyperdetailed game that does not exist.

Graphic motion should feel physical:

  • A control compresses toward its hard shadow.
  • A label stamps into place.
  • A panel slides decisively.
  • A result lands with impact.

Avoid constant floating and ornamental animation. The menu can have attitude; the HUD should report what happened.

7 Intentional imperfection

Good imperfection includes a crude but recognizable bomb drawing, a slightly misregistered headline, an uneven decorative edge, a ridiculous sponsor sign, or a warning label that earns a second look.

Bad imperfection includes random spacing, ambiguous buttons, unreadable cooldowns, inconsistent selection states, effects hiding the opponent, and unrelated assets placed together without curation.

SlopArena should feel improvised, not unattended.

The aim is not expensive polish. It is unmistakable authorship.
